Your First Card Show: What to Expect

By Nathan Wiebe, CPA — collector, and a buyer and seller of cards. Published July 11, 2026.

A card show is just a room full of folding tables, each one rented by a different dealer, all set up for a day or a weekend in a community hall, arena concourse, or hotel ballroom. Most charge a small admission fee at the door, then walk the aisles browsing binders of loose "singles" (individual cards sold on their own, not in a pack or box), display cases of graded cards, and boxes of cheaper "commons" (the everyday base cards that make up most of any set) you're welcome to dig through. Nobody expects you to buy anything, and nobody's tracking how long you browse a table before moving on. If you've only ever bought cards online, the first show can feel like a lot at once — this guide walks through what actually happens, how to handle yourself once you're there, and how to find one near you.

What to Bring

Pack light, but pack a few specific things. Cash in small bills is the single most useful thing in your pocket — more on why below. If you're hunting something specific, bring a written want list so you're not relying on memory table after table. A few penny sleeves and toploaders (rigid plastic holders that protect a card in transit) are worth tossing in a bag so anything you buy survives the trip home loose in your pocket. And if you collect anything valuable enough that condition really matters, a small magnifying loupe (a jeweler's-style handheld magnifier collectors use to check a card's surface up close) lets you check a card properly before you commit, rather than trusting the lighting on a folding table.

Cash vs. Card

Most dealers at a Canadian card show still prefer cash, and plenty will only take cash — a card reader takes a processing cut out of a sale that's often already priced thin, so a lot of vendors would rather skip that entirely. Some tables do accept e-transfer or tap payment through a phone-based card reader, but don't assume it — ask before you're at the register mentally, not after. Don't count on the venue having an ATM on site — bring more cash than you think you'll need rather than counting on finding a machine once you're there.

Handling Cards Politely

Card show etiquette is mostly common sense once someone spells it out. Ask before you pick anything up, even cards sitting loose in a box — it's the dealer's table and their merchandise. Hold cards by the edges only, since the oils on your fingers can leave marks on the surface over time, and that matters a lot more on a card someone's hoping to grade later. If a card's sealed in a hard plastic "toploader" or slabbed in a graded holder, don't pop it out yourself — ask the dealer to show it to you if you want a closer look. Put things back exactly where you found them in the binder or box, and don't crowd a table when someone else is already looking through it. None of this is complicated, but it's the difference between being welcomed back and being the person a dealer watches a little closer next time.

Negotiating Without Being That Guy

Prices marked in a binder or on a box are usually a starting point, not a final number — most dealers expect some back-and-forth and won't be offended by a reasonable counteroffer. There's a real difference, though, between negotiating and lowballing: offering noticeably less than a card is worth, especially without asking any questions about it first, tends to end the conversation fast. You generally get more room to negotiate when you're buying several cards from the same dealer rather than haggling over one bargain-bin card for ten minutes — a small stack gives both of you something to work with. Decide your walk-away price before you're mid-negotiation standing at the table, and it's a lot easier to hold to it.

Spotting an Actual Deal

A deal isn't just a lower number than you expected — it's a price that's genuinely below what the card is trading for right now. Before you assume you've found one, check "comps" (comparable recent sold prices for the same or a very similar card — recently completed eBay listings are the easiest free source) rather than going on a hunch. Condition changes the math too: a card with a soft corner or slightly off centering can be worth meaningfully less than the same card in sharper shape, even though they look nearly identical at a glance across a table. And remember a "raw" card — meaning ungraded, sold on the dealer's word about its condition rather than a third party's — should generally sell for less than the same card already sealed in a graded holder, since the buyer is taking on the condition risk the grading company would otherwise absorb.

Trade Nights and Show Culture

Shows aren't the only place collectors gather. Some local shops run informal "trade nights" — a regular evening set aside for collectors to bring cards and work out trades with each other, usually with less money changing hands than a show and more relationship-building. Trade nights show up in only 17 of our 614 directory listings so far — including Clutch Games in Toronto, ON, TKO Toy Co in Guelph, ON, and Cardboard Memories Inc. in Brampton, ON. Plenty of shops run one without ever listing it anywhere online, so ask your local shop directly — it's a lower-pressure way to get a feel for trading before you ever set foot at a show table.

Finding a Show Near You

Shows run on their own calendar — some annual, some monthly, some one-off — so the best move is checking what's actually coming up rather than guessing.
